# Product-Led / Self-Serve Support

`customer_support.model.plg_self_serve` · model · parent `—`

> Users arrive without ever speaking to anyone, and support is the first human contact the company has with most of them. That single fact reorganises the function. Contact volume tracks the signup and activation curves rather than the installed base, so the queue grows with marketing spend and not with revenue. Most contacts are not defects but comprehension failures — the product did not explain itself — which makes the support queue the highest resolution instrument the product team has and content_gap_analysis a product capability wearing a support badge. Cost to serve is measured against a self-serve price point that cannot absorb a long investigation, so the economics only close if documentation, in-product help and automated answers carry the mass. The habit that breaks here is treating deflection as pure savings. A confused new user deflected into a help article they do not understand is not a saved contact, it is churn with better metrics — and in a self-serve motion nobody will phone to tell you. The inverse error, imported from enterprise, is staffing to answer everything: at these prices a queue built on human throughput has no floor to stand on.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | a self-signed-up user, often on a free or trial plan, frequently evaluating rather than committed |
| typical_resolution_hours | 8 |
| volume_shape | high volume tracking signup and activation curves rather than revenue, spiking on release and on pricing or packaging changes |
| staffing_model | small pooled team behind heavy self-service, generalists with product depth rather than tiers |
| coverage | business hours with explicitly async expectations, set in-product before the contact is made |
| automation_level | very high — docs, in-product help and automated answers are expected to resolve most contacts before a human sees them |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.knowledge_article`


> In this branch the article is not documentation of the resolution, it IS the resolution channel — the primary place a fix is delivered. Coverage, findability and reading level are operational properties here, not editorial ones.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.requester`


> Tenure matters more than seniority. A user in their first session and a user two years in produce identical-looking tickets that mean opposite things: one is an onboarding defect, the other a genuine bug.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.churn_risk`


> Churn here is silent and fast. There is no renewal conversation in which the risk surfaces — the account simply stops being used — so the only leading indicator available is what the user asked and whether they came back.
